probes.support_reason: F-1: every numbered sub-requirement is delivered. (1) `func mid(_ v: [Int]) -> Int { v[1] }` takes one parameter of Swift's normal growable-integer-sequence type -- `[Int]` is the shorthand for `Array<Int>`, the standard library's growable array (TSPL, Collection Types > Array Type Shorthand Syntax) -- and its body returns the element at index 1. (2) `let xs = [1, 2, 3]` binds such a sequence containing 1, 2, 3. (3) `let y = mid(xs)` binds the call's result in Swift's normal binding form. (4) `return y`. F-2: standard library only. F-3: builds and runs under the frozen semantic_compression recipe and prints 2. F-4: no third-party package, no codegen, no flag beyond the recipe. F-6: no normative prohibition or deprecation applies to `Array`, its subscript, or an array literal. R10 alternatives measured with the frozen tokenizer: the chosen form is 37 tokens; `func mid(v: [Int]) ...` with a labelled call `mid(v: xs)` is 38; `{ return v[1] }` instead of the implicit-return body is 38. The 37-token form wins. HIDDEN-COST ADJUDICATION NOTE (methodology 04 section 1.3.0 requires every candidate to be adjudicated, not passed over in silence). H4 was considered twice at this probe and rejected twice. (a) The array literal's heap allocation at local site 2 falls under H4's own exclusion for allocation named by a container literal. (b) The ARC retain of the buffer when `xs` is passed at local site 3, and its release when the values go out of scope, fall under the universal materiality exclusion of section 0.8: no user-visible deinitializer is reachable here (TSPL, Deinitialization confines `deinit` to class types, and neither `Int` nor `Array` is one), and no observer could be built on the frozen host -- `isKnownUniquelyReferenced(_:)` is rejected for `[Int]` with 'requires that [Int] be a class type', and the copy-on-write buffer copy that IS observable through `withUnsafeBufferPointer` requires a mutation, which this fragment never performs. Swift therefore scores 0 for implicit allocation on this probe, which is a real result rather than an oversight. H1, H2, H6, H7, H8 and H9 were likewise adjudicated and rejected: Swift inserts no implicit conversion; a writable alias requires `&`; every reference is non-optional unless written `T?`; no boxing occurs at any site; the fragment contains no arithmetic; and no non-local state is named or reachable. H5 was rejected because the only fallible operation, `v[1]`, is called with the literal index 1 on the three-element `xs` bound inside the fragment, so the out-of-range failure is not reachable in the probe's declared input domain.

A concrete-type extension declared outside the measured fragment shadows `Array.subscript(_: Int)`, so the span may additionally allocate and may not return. VERIFIED WITNESS (methodology 03 Rule 1.3.1): in Swift a declaration in an `extension` on a CONCRETE type outranks the standard library's generic protocol-extension member of the same name and is selected silently, with nothing written at the use site. Built and run on the frozen host: `extension Int32 { static func / (lhs: Int32, rhs: Int32) -> Int32 { return 999 } }` makes `a / b` print 999; the same was confirmed for `*`, `+`, `%`, `<`, `String.==`, `Double.+`, `Array.subscript(Int)`, `Array.sort(by:)`, `Int32.max`, `Int32.init?(exactly:)`, `Int32.addingReportingOverflow(_:)` and `Int32.dividedReportingOverflow(by:)`.
